title: Made All Day, Held Back Until Needed

scenes.tts: Your cells make a protein called p fifty-three all day long. Half of any new batch is destroyed within about twenty minutes. So why build a guardian, only to destroy it? Because a cell in danger cannot wait for a gene to be read and a protein to be built. If the guardian is already there, and something holds it back, the cell only has to let go.
scenes.caption: Your cells make a protein called p53 all day long. Half of any new batch is destroyed within about twenty minutes. So why build a guardian, only to destroy it? scenes.visual: A gene drops p53 chips into a grid of eight. A clock sweeps twenty minutes and four chips turn red and fall into a shredder. A big question mark. A DNA break appears beside two slow grey steps, read the gene then build the protein, with the clock turning and 'cannot wait'. Then the ready chips sit under a hold bar and the bar lifts.

scenes.tts: p fifty-three is a transcription factor, a protein that binds DNA and switches genes on. Its restraint is a protein called M D M two. M D M two grips a short piece at the front end of p fifty-three. That grip covers the part that switches genes on. It also tags p fifty-three with ubiquitin, a mark that sends it to the proteasome to be destroyed.
scenes.caption: p53 is a transcription factor, a protein that binds DNA and switches genes on. Its restraint is a protein called MDM2. MDM2 grips a short piece at the front end of p53. That grip covers the part that switches genes on. It also tags p53 with ubiquitin, a mark that sends it to the proteasome to be destroyed.
scenes.visual: One p53 chip, big, with a green patch at its front end that switches genes on. A purple claw, MDM2, closes over that end and covers the patch. A red ubiquitin tag lands on the chip, the claw opens and the chip slides into the proteasome.

scenes.tts: Now DNA breaks across both strands. That switches on a kinase called A T M. A T M and the kinases beneath it add phosphates to M D M two. They also add phosphates to the stretch of p fifty-three that M D M two grips. The grip loosens, and destruction slows sharply.
scenes.caption: Now DNA breaks across both strands. That switches on a kinase called ATM. ATM and the kinases beneath it add phosphates to MDM2. They also add phosphates to the stretch of p53 that MDM2 grips. The grip loosens, and destruction slows sharply.
scenes.visual: The claw holds p53 again. A double-stranded DNA line breaks across both strands, an ATM chip lights, and gold phosphates fly to the claw and to the front end of p53. The claw loosens and drifts off, the green patch is uncovered, and the road to the proteasome thins to a trickle.

scenes.tts: So p fifty-three piles up without any new gene being read. Free of its restraint, it switches on the gene for p twenty-one. That protein blocks the kinases that drive cell division. It switches on genes for DNA repair as well. If the damage is severe, it also switches on genes that kill the cell.

scenes.visual: The p53 chips pile up in the cell beside a struck-out 'read a new gene' box. They move onto the DNA below and three columns open: the p21 gene turns on and blocks the division kinases, the repair genes turn on, and the cell-death genes light up only under an 'if severe' label.

scenes.tts: Chemical threats use the same design, with a responder called N R F two. N R F two switches on genes for protective enzymes, and the cell makes it constantly. Keap one grips it as part of a ubiquitin ligase that tags it for destruction. Then a reactive chemical hits Keap one. On the current view, tagging stops, so new N R F two goes to the nucleus.
scenes.caption: Chemical threats use the same design, with a responder called Nrf2. Nrf2 switches on genes for protective enzymes, and the cell makes it constantly. Keap1 grips it as part of a ubiquitin ligase that tags it for destruction. Then a reactive chemical hits Keap1. On the current view, tagging stops, so new Nrf2 goes to the nucleus.
scenes.visual: The same shapes again: an Nrf2 chip made by its gene, the purple Keap1 claw closed on it, a red ligase chip taking it away. An orange reactive-chemical chip strikes Keap1, the claw opens, and new Nrf2 drops into a nucleus where the protective-enzyme gene turns green.

scenes.tts: Put the two side by side. In each, a responder is made all the time. Something holds it back, or destroys it. Stress removes the restraint, and the responder is already there. So keep this rule: a stress responder is made all the time and held back, until stress removes the restraint.

scenes.visual: Two rows, p53 with MDM2 and Nrf2 with Keap1, under four headings: made all the time, held back, stress arrives, restraint removed. Each row fills left to right. In both, the orange stress chip arrives, the claw lifts and the chip's patch turns green.
